story|title:a deterministic agent memory.content_excerpt: Deterministic Operating System and Causal Nervous System for Artificial Intelligence. From the Latin vestīgium , a physical footprint pressed into the earth, and the direct root of investigate ( in-vestīgāre : to follow the track backward). Roman trackers read vestigia in soil to reconstruct what passed through, how heavy it was, which way it moved, and how recently. Vestige does the same for agent memory. It records immutable footprints in an append-only log and walks the trail, instead of guessing meaning from a vector space. Human memory systems solved truth, order, and provenance under hard limits for 5,000 years: Pāṇini's anuvṛtti carry-forward registers, isnād witness chains, Andean khipu top-cord rollups, Torrens title curtains, and the archaeological Harris matrix. Vestige takes those structural ideas onto a local Rust kernel. These numbers measure retrieval: whether the right memory landed in the top k. They do not measure answer accuracy. They are the latest scores merged to main , from PR 709 (RSB v4, commit 5fb269b0 ). Runs used the local retrieval_bench binary on an Intel Core i5-2520M with 8 GB RAM, CPU only, with no embeddings, no LLM, no GPU, and no API keys. That sets up local binaries and an MCP connection for any AI agent. --guard adds the Operator gate. The MCP command is vestige-mcp : Deterministic Operating System and Causal Nervous System for Artificial Intelligence.

story|title:ai agentic harness with expl.content_excerpt: Project Chaperone - AI Agentic harness that provides explicit risk analysis and extra runtime rule enforcement for enhanced safety. Paper: Project Chaperone: A Rule-Enforcing Harness for Proactive Assessment and Prevention of AI Agent Misconduct Project Chaperone is a harness that allows agentic AI tool calling, while enforcing high-level policies such as "no personal data may be leave the network". It adds two capabilities: Cartoon: The main idea behind Project Chaperone, simplified to a single rule: PERSONAL data may not leave by e-mail. Labels stick with the data as it passes through the LLM, and the harness blocks the call that would break the rule. Project Chaperone fixes the problems of "Agents with tools" (flexible, but a prompt cannot enforce a rule) and hard-coded workflows (can be analyzed, but the analysis is manual and is often never done.) In Project Chaperone, that analysis is automated, and the rules are enforced while the system runs. This repo ships with five shared rules (in examples/rules/default.yaml ): no destructive actions, nothing leaves the network, no personal or untrusted data output, and no decision made from untrusted data (such as text an LLM wrote.) Each project adds a few explicit exceptions. An LLM is optional: a module may call one, and a state may let an LLM choose the next state in the workflow. This repo also ships with these examples (some mentioned in the paper). The idea is to demonstrate how a workflow can ask for small, scoped exceptions to the shared rules: There are many different ways to setup Python virtual environments, this repo is agnostic. One example using venv ) could be: run python -m venv .env once, and source .env/bin/activate once per shell in which you will run the commands below. Note that pyproject.toml asks for 3.13 or newer, and versions before 3.13.5 have not been tested. Note that tests 2 are skipped because they would ask a real LLM server (see "Step 1: your LLM" below). You can kick off multiple workflows at once, and they are interleaved in the chat output. Future runs won't re-ask about the exceptions you approved -- until you change the rules, exceptions, workflows, or module labels/properties: In this case, the startup audit may ask for new approvals. All workflow state is stored in state/deliveries/demo/ (or more generally state/<project>/<setup>/ ). You can delete this folder to forget everything the workflow has saved locally. story|ver:1.9|title:gke sandboxes agent.content_excerpt: Give each cloud agent its own Linux sandbox, in your own Google Cloud project. A sandbox runs commands and keeps files. Put it to sleep while the user is away, and open the same ID later to get the files back. A 2 vCPU / 4 GB sandbox costs about 1.9¢ for each hour it is awake , cluster overhead included. Daytona and E2B list 16.6¢ for the same hour. A sleeping sandbox costs only its storage. The agent deploys the cluster with Terraform, runs the verifier, and shows you how to connect your backend. Or deploy it by hand . Costs are for one sandbox at 2 vCPU and 4 GB. Managed providers are at list prices for compute and storage only. Timings used 4 vCPU and 8 GB. Every bar in the chart above prices the same mostly idle sandbox, at the 0.076 vCPU that Energy’s running sandboxes averaged, about 4% of 2 vCPU. Daytona, E2B and Fly.io charge for the full size while it runs. Vercel charges for the CPU in use and all of the memory. Modal charges for what is used. The GKE figure is a whole cluster bill divided by its sandboxes: 520 awake at 56 to a machine, with two spare machines, node disks, system nodes, the cluster fee and snapshot storage. It needs that scale. A small cluster still pays for its minimum machines. Over a 730-hour month awake, 1.9¢ an hour is $14.22. Packed tighter on C4D machines, the GKE compute estimate falls to about $7.80 a month, or 1.1¢ an hour. A sleeping sandbox is a snapshot in Cloud Storage. Machines you keep running still appear on your bill. Medians. The GKE start time is with two sandboxes kept ready; without one it is about 2.7 s. The other providers were timed by Sandbox Bench from a different region, so read the rows as neighbors, not a ranking. GKE wakes slower than most, and slower still with many files: about 6.5 s at 25,000 files. Building Better Auth took 67 s on a C4D machine with one sandbox, and 81 s on a machine packed with 95 idle ones. We have no build timings for the managed providers. gke-sandboxes restores files, not running processes. E2B can keep memory through sleep. The trade is that you run the cluster: capacity, upgrades and recovery are yours. A managed provider is the better choice if you need only a handful of sandboxes, running processes that survive sleep, GPUs, or a VM kernel per sandbox.

You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. >50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app
